texts.label: most meaningful impact
texts.text: At Bank of America I built the end-to-end Global Unique Transaction Identifier (GUTI) workflow used to track and report OTC derivatives transactions across global regulatory jurisdictions. The core problem was that million-record trading datasets had to be reported accurately inside strict, time-sensitive regulatory windows, and the existing serial pipeline could not keep up. As the engineer owning the workflow, I designed parallel-processing pipelines partitioned by asset class and region and hardened the system with unit tests and mocks for external API interactions. The result was throughput that met every reporting window and a workflow reliable enough to serve as the backbone of the bank's OTC derivatives regulatory reporting.

texts.label: technically complex problem
texts.text: In my Adscream project I engineered a Go backend that turns a product URL into a finished multi-segment AI video ad. The hard part was orchestrating long-running, failure-prone external providers (Veo/Gemini for video, Gemini TTS, stock footage APIs) into one reliable pipeline. I used NATS JetStream work queues with explicit job-state transitions, crash redelivery, per-segment traceability and provider polling with mock fallbacks, then composed results with FFmpeg. The key tradeoff was synchronous simplicity versus an asynchronous worker architecture; I chose horizontally scalable worker replicas with idempotent state transitions, which made retries safe and let the system survive provider outages without losing customers' paid jobs.

texts.label: main programming languages and technologies
texts.text: Python (primary), Go, TypeScript. Distributed backend services, REST APIs, PostgreSQL, AWS, Docker, message queues (NATS JetStream), CI/CD, and LLM/RAG pipelines.

texts.label: why do you want to join figma
texts.text: Figma's core product is one of the hardest distributed-systems problems in consumer software: real-time multiplayer editing that has to feel instant at massive scale. I've spent seven years building low-latency backend and data systems in finance (BlackRock, Bank of America), and I want to apply that experience to infrastructure that millions of designers and developers feel every day. I also admire how openly Figma's engineering team writes about its technical decisions — the multiplayer protocol, LiveGraph, the databases behind them — and I want to work somewhere that treats that rigor as part of the product.

texts.text: SeatGeek sits at the intersection of live events and serious engineering: high-concurrency onsales, dynamic pricing, and a marketplace where reliability directly decides whether a fan gets into the building. I've spent seven years building low-latency, high-throughput backend systems in finance, and I'd love to point that experience at a product people are genuinely excited about. I also respect how SeatGeek's engineering team writes openly about its platform work — that culture of craft is what I'm looking for.

texts.label: hard technical problems? you have worked on
texts.text: One of the hardest problems I've worked on was rebuilding a portfolio-analytics computation pipeline at BlackRock: risk and performance aggregation across thousands of positions with strict latency budgets. The hard parts were incremental recomputation (avoiding full re-aggregation on every update) and correctness under concurrent updates — solved with a dependency-graph scheduler and idempotent, versioned computation steps. More recently I've built LLM/RAG pipelines where the real engineering problems were retrieval quality, evaluation, and cost control rather than the model calls themselves.
